title: The Senate Votes to Make Data Centers Pay. Florida Floods Again. Mortgage Rates Climb.
subject: The Senate Votes to Make Data Centers Pay. Florida Floods Again. Mortgage Rates Climb.
preview_text: An energy bill heads to the House, the Space Coast floods, and home loans get pricier again.
description: The Senate passes a bill making data centers pay for power, storms flood Florida, and mortgage rates rise again.
contents_extra: Why the first US deep-sea mining leases are headed to court, trivia and your poll

stories.title: The Senate Passes an Energy Bill That Makes Data Centers Pay for Power

photo.alt: Power line tower against a gray sky; file photo.

paragraphs: The Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday to speed up permitting for power plants, transmission lines and other energy projects, the AP reports. The bill would also make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. It now goes to the House.

CNBC reports the bill is projected to lower energy costs for consumers while weakening some environmental laws. More than a dozen Democrats, including Chuck Schumer, voted yes. Opponents lamented rollbacks to bedrock environmental protection laws, CNBC reports.

stories.title: Record Rain Floods Florida as Storms Move Up the Space Coast

photo.alt: Floodwater covering a residential street; file photo.

paragraphs: Storms shifted north to Florida's Space Coast on Thursday, prompting nearly 100 high-water rescues in Brevard County, NBC News reports, citing the AP. The Fort Lauderdale area got nearly 17 inches of rain in 48 hours, according to preliminary weather service totals.

ABC News reports the St. Johns River near Cocoa rose above record levels. The National Hurricane Center gave the system a 60% chance of becoming tropical or subtropical this weekend. A flood threat stretches from Daytona Beach to Charleston on Saturday.

stories.title: The Average 30-Year Mortgage Rate Rises to 7.28% After a Four-Week Slide

photo.alt: Gray house with palm trees in Florida; file photo.

paragraphs: The average 30-year mortgage rate rose to 7.28% from 7.11%, Freddie Mac said Thursday, according to the AP. It was the first weekly increase since early October. A year ago, the average was 6.26%.

The 15-year rate climbed to 6.66% from 6.45%, ABC News reports. Rates track the 10-year Treasury yield, which was 5.05% at midday Thursday. Signs of hotter inflation have raised the odds of a Fed rate hike in December.

stories.title: The White House Names a New Cyber Chief After a Week of Outages

photo.alt: Server racks in a data center; file photo.

paragraphs: The White House named Kirsten Davies as national cyber director on Thursday after widespread service outages, the AP reports. Davies is the Defense Department's chief information officer. She replaces Sean Cairncross.

A source told NBC News Davies will serve in an acting capacity. The post requires Senate confirmation. Officials and some Democrats have said the outages do not appear to be cyberattacks, NBC reports.

deep_dive.title: The US Sells Its First Deep-Sea Mining Leases, and the Lawsuits Follow

photo.alt: Sandy seabed with rocks and fish; file photo.

paragraphs: What happened. The Trump administration auctioned two deep-sea mining leases near American Samoa on Thursday, the AP reports. Startup Wetstone U.S. Ventures won both at the $3 million minimum bid each. The 20-year leases are the first of their kind in the U.S. They cover millions of acres of federal seafloor.

Why it matters. The Interior Department says the two areas cover about 31.5 million acres at depths of 4,630 to 20,100 feet. It calls the sale a step for mineral security. Critical minerals are used in electronics and defense systems. Globally, no company has started commercial deep-sea mining, according to the AP.

What each side says. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum called it a historic step for American mineral security, the department said. Earthjustice says a court ruling on Monday made the auction unlawful. Its attorney Chris Eaton said the group will push for the leases to be voided. An industry group expects interest and investment to grow.

What comes next. The leases let Wetstone begin seafloor surveys, the AP reports. Commercial mining would need approval in further environmental reviews. Three lawsuits seek to halt or strike down the sales. The Marine Minerals Administration is considering further auctions near the Northern Mariana Islands, Virginia and Alaska, the AP reports.

World view: Italy walks off the job. A 24-hour CGIL union strike was expected to disrupt schools, hospitals and transport. Protests were planned in more than 100 cities; AP reports.

Saudi Arabia reports new Houthi attacks. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a ballistic missile and five drones Friday morning, days after air strikes in Yemen. The Houthis did not immediately claim the attacks; AP reports.
Bukele registers for a third term. El Salvador's president filed his candidacy for February elections after term limits were removed; Al Jazeera reports.
Gaza rescuers run short of working vehicles. Civil Defence says over 85 percent of its vehicles are out of service. One crew ran to a strike site on foot; Al Jazeera reports.
Need to know: No charges in a Madison police shooting. A prosecutor said the officer who killed Corey Ruiz in July acted reasonably, drawing condemnation from his family; NBC News reports.
Climate talks may back carbon removal. UN negotiators at COP31 in Turkey are likely to say the world must pull carbon from the air; AP reports.
Meta rethinks its 2030 net-zero goal. The company said it is re-evaluating its timelines after emissions rose 45% in 2025 amid the AI boom; Al Jazeera reports.
Meta staff flag a privacy problem. Employees say its AI agent Muse mixed up conversations and surfaced other people's data, according to a Reuters report; TechCrunch reports.
Money & markets: Futures slip before Friday's open. Early Friday, S&P 500 futures were down 0.37% and Nasdaq-100 futures 0.88% after a 2%-plus drop Thursday; CNBC reports.
Anthropic falls in premarket trading. The stock was down 5.6% at 4:23 a.m. ET, a day after a 17% first-day gain; CNBC reports.
SoftBank has its worst day since 2024. Its shares closed 14.48% lower Friday as an AI sell-off swept Asian tech stocks; CNBC reports.

Chase vendors are hit by a cyberattack. JPMorganChase said attackers accessed marketing data held by vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses. Services are not disrupted; ABC News reports.
Future frontiers: Gemini can now use your Mac. Google is adding computer use to its macOS app, so its AI can work across apps and websites; TechCrunch reports.
SpaceX designs a rooftop mini cell tower. Elon Musk said the towers, aimed at indoor dead zones, are expected to enter production in 2027; TechCrunch reports.
Perseverance pauses its science work. NASA says the Mars rover is stable while teams work on problems with its two UHF radios; NASA says.
NASA tests an engine for future Artemis missions. A developmental RS-25 engine, which will not be used in flight, ran for 200 seconds in a Nov. 18 test at Stennis Space Center; NASA says.
The score: Mark Stone sets a Vegas record. The captain's 418th point made him the Golden Knights' career scoring leader in a shootout loss to Dallas; ESPN reports.
Antonelli gets a grid penalty in Las Vegas. The new F1 champion drops five places for a new engine, while George Russell topped wet second practice; ESPN reports.
Houston beats Kansas 92-83. The No. 8 Cougars won the Players Era 8 final and could rise to No. 1 in Monday's AP poll; ESPN reports.
Lakshya Sen reaches the Hong Kong Open semis. He beat former world champion Loh Kean Yew to extend a 13-match winning streak; ESPN reports.
Life & culture: Fiona the hippo dies. The Cincinnati Zoo said she could not overcome a knit hat she swallowed after it landed in her enclosure; CBS News reports.
Pitcher-turned-actor Lance Broadway dies at 43. The former White Sox and Mets pitcher died Tuesday in Dallas; the cause was not immediately clear; AP reports.
A Commanders quarterback will be "The Bachelor." Practice-squad QB Sam Hartman will star in the show's 30th season, which premieres March 21; AP reports.
CBS keeps the Kennedy Center Honors. Sources say a one-year deal will air the gala on Dec. 27 from Capital One Arena; CBS News reports.

trivia.question: How long are the first US deep-sea mining leases?
trivia.explanation: C. 20 years. The AP reports the two leases near American Samoa run for 20 years and are the first of their kind in the U.S.

poll.question: Should data centers pay more of the cost of new power plants and lines?
